articleTitle: IEE Colloquium on 'The T9000 Transputer' (Digest No.1994/208)

abstract: Since its introduction in 1985, the transputer has been used for a variety of diverse applications from single processor GPS (Global Positioning System) consumer products to MPP (Massively Parallel Processor) applications. What is clear is that although these applications are using essentially the same part, the requirements on the processor are very different. The result is that some of the general purpose features used by one application may not necessarily be used by another, and hence excess features may exist in the device. Microprocessor designs have become very complex, requiring large design teams and significant investment to realise the latest "hot chip". The design cycle times of our customers are becoming shorter as markets become more competitive and time to market is a critical issue. This is forcing companies like SGS-THOMSON to become more responsive to customer demands and optimise microprocessor design for specific applications. The author presents three key factors which affect whether a microprocessor development will produce acceptable first silicon in a timeframe which will support the market.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

Distributed systems are incapable of handling certain problems which cannot be broken down into sub-problems without the use of communications bandwidths which such systems cannot provide. If this bandwidth can be provided, however, as in a scaleable massively parallel system then significant parallelism can be found in such applications. In particular Relational Database Management Systems (RDBMSs) have been shown to be capable of being parallelised in this way. Often it is then possible to encapsulate most of the difficult parts of parallelising a business application inside the RDBMS, leaving the remainder of the application as multitasking sequential code which can be distributed if necessary. Oracle was the first RDBMS vendor to recognise this and Parsys has been working with them since 1989 to implement their system, firstly on the T800 transputer and now the T9000. The author looks at how this has been acheived.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Software development with the IMS T9000
abstract: This paper discusses the process of developing applications for the IMS T9000. It gives a general overview of the development process, types of tool required, and discusses aspects of software development and debugging specific to multi-processor, and multi-threaded applications.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Application of transputer links and routers in telecommunication systems
abstract: This paper is concerned with the developments and trends in telecommunication systems over the past few years. It discusses the development of a generic model that can be applied to communications architectures and how switching has become a major aspect of all wide area and local area networking methodologies. It goes on to show the use of transputer links and associated routing devices in various applications and what benefits can be gained through the use of this technology.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Image processing applications on the T9000 transputer
abstract: Quintek specialise in real-time applications of transputers for image processing. Quintek has developed PC-based image processing systems based on the HarleQuin and MosaiQ frame-capture boards. Our prime T9000 product is ConQueror, which is a multi-channel camera system designed for transport surveillance. Each camera is fitted with a T9000-based capture module, the QT9C HTRAM and all are linked together in a united network with a display module, the QT9D. Quintek has concentrated its image processing applications in the surveillance of transport systems: road traffic, rail freight, dockyards and car parks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: T9000s performing image enhancement in high end graphic arts input scanner
abstract: ICG (formerly known as Itek Colour Graphics) is a small company, which supplies high quality capital equipment to the colour printing market. Over a period of more than 20 years ICG has manufactured machines for scanning colour images and for outputting separations. The latest ICG input scanner is the 350i. The design criteria set at the start of the 350i development project were very challenging. The objectives were to develop a new machine in one year rather than two and to minimise build cost, without any technical compromise. Radical technical solutions were required to satisfy these demanding criteria. A selection of alternative RISC systems was considered from which the T9000 was chosen. The author looks at the scanner, and some of the design issues considered.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A T9000 simulation of the human peripheral hearing system
abstract: This paper presents new work on the implementation of a contemporary model of the human peripheral hearing system. The model presented runs in real-time on a system using T800 and T9000 transputers and overcomes many of the problems found with a previous T800-based system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

The development of new microprocessors is being influenced by a number of key factors. This paper captures some of these factors and highlights why they must be considered in the fast moving consumer electronics market.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Parallel discrete event simulation on a T9000 transputer network
abstract: Discrete event simulation provides a method of studying the behaviour of large systems by conducting experiments on a computer-based model rather than on the physical system itself. It is an important tool in the design of new systems such as industrial plants, road traffic networks or computer architectures, as it provides the designer with a way of modelling and analyzing the behaviour of such systems before their physical construction takes place. Traditionally, discrete event simulation has been performed in a sequential manner but the size and complexity of many of today's simulation models demand a move towards parallel execution.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
